layoutData.tagline: Established Regional Carrier with Diversified Service Platform

layoutData.body:
Pacific Coast Logistics Ltd. is a well-established regional transportation and logistics company serving the Lower Mainland, Fraser Valley and Pacific Northwest from its 110,000 square foot facility in Surrey, British Columbia. Founded in 1991 and incorporated in 1998, the company has built a 34-year track record of reliable service through a diversified mix of dry van and temperature-controlled trucking, port drayage, and third-party warehousing and cross-dock operations.

The business operates a fleet of 71 power units and 160 trailers, supported by modern warehouse infrastructure that includes 12,400 pallet positions with 3,100 positions in a temperature-controlled cooler. This combination of transportation and warehousing capabilities positions Pacific Coast as a comprehensive logistics partner for food distributors, building supply companies, beverage manufacturers, and other shippers across British Columbia.

Pacific Coast serves over 300 active customers, with its largest account representing 22 percent of revenue under a master service agreement running through 2027. The top five customers account for 47 percent of annual volume, while the remaining business is distributed across nearly 300 smaller accounts. Food-related freight represents approximately 50 percent of total revenue, reflecting the company's strength in temperature-controlled logistics and its long-standing relationships with grocery and produce distributors.

The company demonstrated exceptional resilience during the November 2021 British Columbia floods, when highway closures severed supply routes across the province. Pacific Coast kept its anchor grocery customer's stores supplied by running trucks through back roads and mountain passes, with drivers sleeping in their cabs to maintain delivery schedules. This performance during a critical supply chain disruption strengthened customer relationships that in many cases span two decades or more.

Today, the business employs 148 people, including 96 company drivers, 30 warehouse staff, 7 in dispatch and load planning, 6 shop personnel, and a management team with deep industry experience. The operation is supported by modern systems including Axon transportation management software, Samsara electronic logging and telematics, and Magaya warehouse management with customer portal access.

left.title: Customer Diversification
left.content:
Pacific Coast Logistics serves a diversified base of over 300 active customers across British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest. The customer portfolio spans food distribution and grocery, building supply, beverage, pet food, furniture, and dairy sectors, with food-related freight representing approximately 50 percent of total business.

The company has built its reputation on reliability and customer service over 34 years of operation. Many key relationships span 20 to 25 years, with the anchor customer, Alderbrook Grocery Distributors, having been served since 2009. The business demonstrated exceptional loyalty during the 2021 BC floods, when Pacific Coast kept Alderbrook stores supplied by routing trucks through back roads, with drivers working around the clock to maintain deliveries.

This proven track record through supply chain disruptions has strengthened customer relationships and positioned the company as a trusted logistics partner. The diversified customer base provides revenue stability while maintaining meaningful scale with anchor accounts that value long-term partnership and operational excellence.

left.title: Workforce Profile
left.content:
Pacific Coast Logistics employs 96 company drivers as of December 31, 2024, comprising 82 full-time and 14 part-time or spare-board drivers. All drivers are employees, not owner-operators, eliminating misclassification risk.

The driver roster is divided into four operational groups: 38 linehaul and regional highway drivers (34 full-time, 4 part-time), 26 city and regional distribution drivers (21 full-time, 5 part-time), 18 dedicated reefer drivers for grocery accounts (16 full-time, 2 part-time), and 14 port drayage drivers (11 full-time, 3 part-time).

Average driver tenure is just over six years, with 24 drivers having more than 10 years of service. The longest-tenured driver has been with the company for 26.8 years, hired in March 1998.

All 96 drivers hold Class 1 licences with air brake endorsement and TDG (Transportation of Dangerous Goods) certification. Twenty-two drivers hold FAST cards for cross-border operations into Washington State.

Linehaul drivers are paid $0.64 to $0.73 per kilometre plus hourly pay for delays exceeding two hours, with a $25 drop and hook fee and a $0.02 per kilometre safe-driving bonus paid quarterly. City, reefer and drayage drivers earn $30.50 to $36.50 per hour, with overtime paid after 60 hours per week under the BC motor carrier variance.

Full-time drivers averaged approximately $74,000 in gross earnings in 2024. Benefits include extended health and dental coverage, a 3 percent RRSP match, and a $2,500 referral bonus for any driver who refers a new hire retained for six months. Most new hires come through referrals.

Quarterly driver town halls were introduced following the 2023 union certification vote, which failed 38 in favour to 51 against. The safe-driving bonus program was also introduced post-vote.

layoutData.body:
Pacific Coast Logistics experiences a pronounced seasonal pattern in both trucking and warehousing operations, driven primarily by the grocery and retail supply chain cycles that form the core of the business.

The fourth quarter represents the company's strongest period, accounting for approximately 28 percent of annual revenue. This peak is driven by holiday grocery volumes through the Alderbrook relationship and broader retail restocking activity as customers build inventory ahead of the year-end shopping season. Both the temperature-controlled fleet and the warehouse facility operate at or near capacity during these months, and spot rates for overflow freight improve materially.

The first quarter is the year's slowest period, typically representing roughly 22 percent of annual revenue. General freight demand softens following the holiday peak, and winter weather closures on the Coquihalla Highway and Highway 3 reduce available operating days and increase transit times. Customers defer non-urgent shipments during this period, and the company uses the slower months for equipment maintenance, driver training refreshers, and system improvements.

The summer months bring a lift on the temperature-controlled side of the business, as BC's produce season generates increased reefer demand for the movement of fresh fruits and vegetables. This seasonal strength partially offsets the post-holiday softness in other freight categories and helps smooth the revenue curve between the first-quarter trough and the fourth-quarter peak.

Warehousing revenue follows a similar pattern to trucking, with the same fourth-quarter peak and first-quarter trough. Storage utilization climbs through the fall as customers build safety stock, and handling volumes increase with higher throughput. Cross-dock activity for holiday imports peaks in October and November, then drops sharply in January and February.

The business has managed this seasonality successfully for decades. The driver workforce includes a roster of part-time and spare-board drivers who absorb the peak-season volume without requiring year-round payroll, and the warehouse layout allows the company to flex labor and equipment to match demand. Seasonal cash flow is predictable, and the company maintains its operating line to smooth working capital through the first-quarter trough.

left.title: Recent Capital Investment
left.content:
Pacific Coast Logistics has maintained a disciplined capital investment program, with total additions of $3,960,000 in FY2022, $3,240,000 in FY2023, and $2,860,000 in FY2024. The company cycles highway tractors on a 5-6 year replacement schedule, maintaining a modern fleet while optimizing residual values through strategic disposals.

FY2022 capital spending included the initial build-out of the Campbell Ridge facility, with significant investment in warehouse racking, the 22,000 square foot temperature-controlled cooler, office improvements, and leasehold work to prepare the new building for operations.

FY2023 investments focused on fleet expansion to support warehousing growth, including tractors, refrigerated trailers, forklifts, and container chassis. The company also invested in technology infrastructure and systems to support operational scale.

FY2024 capital expenditures included freight tractors and trucks totaling $1,580,000, trailers and chassis totaling $850,000, warehouse equipment and racking totaling $210,000, computer hardware and software totaling $120,000, and leasehold improvements totaling $100,000. The year also included the migration to the Axon transportation management system, representing approximately $72,000 in one-time consulting costs.

right.title: Near-Term Capital Requirements
right.content:
The fleet includes 14 refrigerated trailers from 2011-2014 that have reached 11-14 years of age and require replacement over the next 12-18 months. Management estimates this reefer replacement program at approximately $1,400,000.

Beyond the aging reefer trailer replacement, the company's normal maintenance capital expenditure runs between $2,300,000 and $2,600,000 annually, supporting the replacement of 8-12 highway tractors each year on the established 5-6 year cycle. Day cab tractors used for port drayage are typically operated longer, at 8-9 years, due to lower annual mileage accumulation.

Management's 24-month capital budget totals approximately $6,000,000 to $7,000,000, encompassing the reefer trailer replacement program plus normal fleet renewal and ongoing warehouse equipment needs. Two battery-electric day cab units are on order for mid-2026 delivery with provincial incentive support, representing the company's initial investment in electric vehicle technology for urban and port operations.

The company's equipment financing relationships with Pacific Crest Equipment Finance Ltd. and Westshore Commercial Bank provide established access to capital for ongoing fleet renewal. Sixteen leased highway tractors from Westline were rolled over to new 2022-2024 model year units during the recent replacement cycle.

layoutData.body:
After 34 years in the transportation industry and 27 years at the helm of Pacific Coast Logistics, the founder and majority owner has decided to pursue succession. The company was incorporated in 1998 and has grown from a regional carrier into a diversified logistics operation with trucking, temperature-controlled transport, and warehousing capabilities serving over 300 customers across British Columbia.

The business is being sold as a going concern with all systems, contracts, relationships, and personnel in place. The 110,000-square-foot facility in Surrey is held under a lease running through September 2037, and the major customer contracts—including the master service agreement with the largest account that extends to March 2027—transfer with the transaction.

The owner's daughter, Manpreet Grewal, currently serves as VP Operations and has been with the company for 13 years. Manpreet has indicated a willingness to remain in the business for a minimum of two to three years post-sale in a general manager or VP Operations capacity, and is open to rolling 10 to 15 percent of proceeds into the acquiring entity if the buyer is the right partner—specifically a larger carrier or a private-equity-backed platform building out Western Canada.

The sale timeline contemplated by the owner was to complete a transaction within approximately one year. The company has retained advisory support and is positioned for a smooth transition to new ownership with deep operational continuity and management succession already in place.

items.description: A buyer who recognizes the strategic value of the warehousing operation, which grew 35.5 percent from 2022 to 2024 and now represents 22 percent of total revenue. 1. Nature of operations
Pacific  Coast  Logistics  Ltd.  (the  "Company")  was  incorporated  on  June  3,  1998  under  the  Company  Act  (British

2. Significant accounting policies
These  financial  statements  have  been  prepared  in  accordance  with  Canadian  accounting  standards  for  private  
enterprises (ASPE) and include the following significant accounting policies:
•  Revenue  recognition  —  Freight  revenue,  including  fuel  surcharges,  is  recognized  when  the  delivery  is  completed.  
Warehousing  storage  revenue  is  recognized  monthly  as  the  service  is  provided;  handling  and  cross-dock  revenue  is  
recognized when the services are performed.
•  Inventory — Fuel, parts and tires are valued at the lower of cost (first-in, first-out) and net realizable value.
•  Property  and  equipment  —  recorded  at  cost  less  accumulated  amortization.  Amortization  is  provided  as  follows:  
tractors  and  trucks  —  straight-line  over  6  years  to  an  estimated  residual  value  of  30%  of  cost;  trailers  and  container  
chassis — straight-line over 15 years to an estimated residual value of 20% of cost; warehouse equipment, racking and 
forklifts, and shop and yard equipment — 20% declining balance; computer hardware and software — 45% declining 
balance;  office  furniture  and  fixtures  —  20%  declining  balance;  leasehold  improvements  —  straight-line  over  the  
remaining term of the lease. One-half of the normal amortization is recorded in the year of acquisition.
• Income taxes — The Company follows the future income taxes method. Future income taxes arise principally from 
differences between the carrying value of property and equipment and its undepreciated capital cost for tax purposes.
• Leases — Leases are classified as capital or operating leases. The warehouse premises and 19 leased tractors are 
accounted for as operating leases; payments are expensed as incurred.
•  Use  of  estimates  —  The  preparation  of  financial  statements  requires  management  to  make  estimates  that  affect  
reported  amounts.  Significant  estimates  include  the  useful  lives  of  property  and  equipment  and  the  allowance  for

These  financial  statements  have  been  prepared  in  accordance  with  Canadian  accounting  standards  for  private  
enterprises (ASPE) and include the following significant accounting policies:
•  Revenue  recognition  —  Freight  revenue,  including  fuel  surcharges,  is  recognized  when  the  delivery  is  completed.

recognized when the services are performed.

differences between the carrying value of property and equipment and its undepreciated capital cost for tax purposes.

accounted for as operating leases; payments are expensed as incurred.

1. Nature of operations
Pacific  Coast  Logistics  Ltd.  (the  "Company")  was  incorporated  on  June  3,  1998  under  the  Company  Act  (British  
Columbia) and continued under the Business Corporations Act (British Columbia). The Company provides regional 
truckload transportation (dry van and temperature-controlled), port container drayage, and third-party warehousing 
and cross-dock services from its facility in Surrey, British Columbia.
2. Significant accounting policies
These  financial  statements  have  been  prepared  in  accordance  with  Canadian  accounting  standards  for  private  
enterprises (ASPE) and include the following significant accounting policies:
•  Revenue  recognition  —  Freight  revenue,  including  fuel  surcharges,  is  recognized  when  the  delivery  is  completed.  
Warehousing  storage  revenue  is  recognized  monthly  as  the  service  is  provided;  handling  and  cross-dock  revenue  is  
recognized when the services are performed.
•  Inventory — Fuel, parts and tires are valued at the lower of cost (first-in, first-out) and net realizable value.
•  Property  and  equipment  —  recorded  at  cost  less  accumulated  amortization.  Amortization  is  provided  as  follows:  
tractors  and  trucks  —  straight-line  over  6  years  to  an  estimated  residual  value  of  30%  of  cost;  trailers  and  container  
chassis — straight-line over 15 years to an estimated residual value of 20% of cost; warehouse equipment, racking and 
forklifts, and shop and yard equipment — 20% declining balance; computer hardware and software — 45% declining 
balance;  office  furniture  and  fixtures  —  20%  declining  balance;  leasehold  improvements  —  straight-line  over  the  
remaining term of the lease. One-half of the normal amortization is recorded in the year of acquisition.
• Income taxes — The Company follows the future income taxes method. Future income taxes arise principally from 
differences between the carrying value of property and equipment and its undepreciated capital cost for tax purposes.
• Leases — Leases are classified as capital or operating leases. The warehouse premises and 19 leased tractors are 
accounted for as operating leases; payments are expensed as incurred.
•  Use  of  estimates  —  The  preparation  of  financial  statements  requires  management  to  make  estimates  that  affect  
reported  amounts.  Significant  estimates  include  the  useful  lives  of  property  and  equipment  and  the  allowance  for  
doubtful accounts.
